sourceText: The MEMETIC-QUARANTINE sector was already in progress when they entered. For several lessons Aster had refused to pause worlds for their arrival; the fact that a class was visiting was not a cosmic event for the inhabitants. A short sentence creates a compulsive urge to be transmitted despite containing no good argument. The memorial bore the name of Stephenson; infohazard traditions precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Information was not merely something that circulated between agents. Sometimes it changed the agent, sometimes the environment, and in the most dangerous cases it changed the criterion by which truth could be recognized. Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along. At the center of the conflict was Sael, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that 213 had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: Marae infects herself voluntarily and discovers that, from the inside, the impulse feels like her own conviction. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Mm — Memetic Agent: information reproduces by modifying its reader; Ba — Informational Basilisk: perceiving a pattern creates risk. Course references included memetic SF; information-hazard fiction. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Vela broke the first consensus. ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ Marae answered without raising their voice: ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build 214 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. Aster admits that the White Hunger has a similar structure: a desire that presents itself as an epistemic necessity. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the GENESIS operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — allows a system to create new agents, worlds, laws, or substrates — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, 215 and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 216 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS 217 PART 8​ INSTITUTIONS OF THE IMPOSSIBLE A period in the curriculum of the five children 218 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
